concepts.name: Definition and Rationale of Small Finance Banks (SFBs)
key_dimensions: Distinction from universal banks, payment banks, and cooperative banks
Core objective: financial inclusion for unserved/underserved segments
Historical context: Nachiket Mor Committee recommendations and RBI 2014 policy paper
Why SFBs were preferred over Regional Rural Banks (RRBs) or Local Area Banks (LABs) for inclusion goals

concepts.name: Licensing Framework and Eligibility Criteria for SFBs
key_dimensions: Minimum paid-up capital requirement: Rs. 200 crore (trap: differentiate from payment banks at Rs. 100 crore)
Eligible promoters: resident individuals, NBFCs, MFIs, LABs — not large industrial houses
Fit and proper criteria for promoters and the 5-year residency requirement
On-tap licensing introduced in 2019 vs. original 2015 window — implications for entry

concepts.name: Mandatory Priority Sector Lending (PSL) Targets for SFBs
key_dimensions: 75% of Adjusted Net Bank Credit (ANBC) to priority sector — trap: higher than universal banks (40%)
Sub-target: 40% of ANBC to loans up to Rs. 25 lakh for small and marginal farmers, micro enterprises
How SFBs can achieve PSL through inter-bank participation certificates or PSLC trading
Comparison with RRBs (75% PSL) and cooperative banks to identify overlaps

concepts.name: Deposit and Lending Restrictions Specific to SFBs
key_dimensions: SFBs can accept all types of deposits (CASA, FD, RD) — key distinction from payment banks
75% of loan portfolio must consist of loans up to Rs. 25 lakh (microfinance focus)
No restriction on interest rates on deposits — can offer higher rates to attract deposits
Cannot set up subsidiaries for non-banking financial activities without RBI approval

concepts.name: Capital Adequacy and Prudential Norms for SFBs
key_dimensions: Minimum Capital to Risk-weighted Assets Ratio (CRAR): 15% — trap: higher than 9% for universal banks
Tier-1 capital requirement of at least 7.5%
SFBs are subject to full Basel III norms like universal banks
Concentration risk: higher exposure norms scrutiny due to narrow target segment

concepts.name: Promoter Shareholding and Dilution Requirements
key_dimensions: Initial lock-in: promoter must hold minimum 40% for first 5 years
Mandatory listing on stock exchange within 3 years of reaching net worth of Rs. 500 crore
Long-run promoter cap: shareholding to be brought down to 26% within 12 years
Trap: Foreign shareholding norms — follow FDI policy for private sector banks (74% cap under automatic route)

concepts.name: Transition Pathway: SFB to Universal Bank
key_dimensions: RBI guidelines (2019/2021): SFB can apply for universal bank license after 5 years of satisfactory operation
Eligibility conditions: minimum net worth Rs. 1,000 crore, listed, CRAR compliance, net NPA below 3%
Trap: Not automatic — subject to RBI's discretionary approval
First mover: AU Small Finance Bank's application as a case study

concepts.name: Branch Network and Operational Area Requirements
key_dimensions: At least 25% of branches must be in unbanked rural centres (population less than 9,999)
No geographic restriction — SFBs can operate pan-India (distinguish from LABs which were restricted)
Digital banking units and BC network as tools to meet rural outreach without physical branches
Comparison: RRBs restricted to notified districts; SFBs have no such restriction

concepts.name: Payment Banks vs. Small Finance Banks: Critical Comparisons
key_dimensions: Payment banks cannot lend; SFBs can both lend and accept deposits — most common UPSC trap
Payment banks: max deposit Rs. 2 lakh per customer; SFBs: no such cap
Payment banks focus on remittances and payments; SFBs focus on credit to micro/small segments
Promoter eligibility overlap: telecom companies can be payment bank promoters but not SFB promoters

concepts.name: SFBs and Microfinance Institutions (MFI) Nexus
key_dimensions: Several SFBs converted from NBFC-MFIs (e.g., Bandhan, Ujjivan, Equitas)
Trap: After conversion, MFI income ceiling norms no longer apply but PSL targets kick in
Dual regulation risk: legacy MFI clients under RBI's MFI regulation vs. SFB's own credit policies
RBI's harmonised MFI regulations (2022) and their impact on SFB lending practices

concepts.name: Deposit Insurance Coverage for SFB Depositors
key_dimensions: DICGC coverage: Rs. 5 lakh per depositor per bank — same as universal banks (post-2020 amendment)
Significance for SFB depositors who are typically low-income and risk-averse
Trap: Coverage is per depositor per bank, not per account — important nuance
DICGC Act 1961 amendment (2021): timeline for payment within 90 days of liquidation

concepts.name: RBI's Supervisory and Regulatory Oversight of SFBs
key_dimensions: SFBs licensed under Section 22 of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949 — same as universal banks
Subject to RBI's Prompt Corrective Action (PCA) framework
Reporting requirements: SFBs submit returns under the same framework as scheduled commercial banks
Trap: SFBs scheduled under 2nd Schedule of RBI Act — eligible for refinance from RBI and SIDBI

concepts.name: Financial Inclusion Mandate vs. Commercial Viability Tension
key_dimensions: High cost of funds (no large corporate deposits) vs. low ticket size loans — profitability squeeze
NPA vulnerability: client base (small farmers, MFI borrowers) exposed to income shocks
NABARD/SIDBI refinance facilities as cost-reduction tools for SFBs
COVID-19 stress test: SFBs' performance compared to universal banks highlights systemic risks

concepts.name: Technology and Business Correspondent (BC) Model in SFBs
key_dimensions: BCs used to extend last-mile credit and deposit services without physical branches
Jan Dhan, Aadhaar, Mobile (JAM) trinity integration for KYC and direct benefit transfer
RBI guidelines on BC liability: bank remains responsible for BC actions
Trap: SFBs can use BCs but payment banks rely more heavily on digital/BC model — different risk profiles

concepts.name: SFBs' Role in Agricultural Credit and NABARD Linkages
key_dimensions: SFBs eligible for NABARD refinance for agricultural and rural lending
Kisan Credit Card (KCC) issuance by SFBs to meet PSL sub-targets
Distinction: SFBs compete with Regional Rural Banks in rural credit but are privately owned
SFBs vs. cooperative banks in short-term agricultural credit — structural advantage of SFBs

concepts.name: Scheduled Status and Access to Money Markets
key_dimensions: SFBs included in 2nd Schedule of RBI Act — eligible for CRR maintenance and SLR requirements
Access to Marginal Standing Facility (MSF), Repo, and Reverse Repo windows from Day 1
Trap: SFBs must maintain CRR (4%) and SLR (18%) like universal banks — same statutory pre-emptions
Call money market and CBLO access for liquidity management

concepts.name: Governance Requirements and Board Composition of SFBs
key_dimensions: Majority of directors must be independent; at least half the board should have banking/finance expertise
Mandatory full-time MD & CEO with RBI approval — no part-time CEO allowed
Fit and Proper criteria under RBI's Corporate Governance guidelines for banks
Trap: Promoter cannot be MD&CEO beyond 15 years — succession planning obligation

concepts.name: Current Account and SFBs: The Interoperability Dimension
key_dimensions: RBI's Current Account Circular (2020): SFBs affected by restrictions on opening current accounts for borrowers of other banks
SFBs' competitive disadvantage in cash management services vs. large banks
UPI and IMPS interoperability allowing SFBs to compete in digital payments ecosystem
Trap: SFBs can issue credit cards (unlike payment banks) — expanding product suite

concepts.name: Foreign Portfolio Investment (FPI) and Foreign Direct Investment (FDI) in SFBs
key_dimensions: FDI up to 74% permitted under automatic route (same as private sector banks)
Beyond 74% requires government approval — trap: no separate FDI policy for SFBs vs. universal banks
FPI investment subject to sectoral caps and SEBI regulations post-listing
Impact of foreign ownership on financial inclusion mandate — regulatory concern

concepts.name: Performance and Evolution: SFB Sector Assessment
key_dimensions: Bandhan Bank's conversion to universal bank (2019) as a policy precedent
Concerns raised: SFBs concentrating in urban/semi-urban areas, deviating from rural inclusion mandate
RBI's review and tightening of on-tap licensing norms post-2021
Trap: Not all applicants who received in-principle approval converted to SFBs — lapsed approvals (e.g., initial 2015 list of 10 applicants)
